title: January Bonsai Checklist
intro: January is generally the heart of winter, with very little active work to do on dormant bonsai. The priority now is protecting trees from extreme cold while keeping an eye on moisture and winter conditions.

sections.heading: Winter Protection
items: Make sure all trees that need winter protection are safely sheltered.
A cold greenhouse is ideal, but a simple winter shelter can work just as well.
Protect trees from prolonged exposure to extreme cold, strong winds, frost and heavy snow.
Keep in mind that bonsai containers are much more vulnerable to freezing than trees growing in the ground.
Check your shelters after major storms to make sure they are still secure and providing adequate protection.
Avoid allowing the shelter to become too warm on sunny days. Trees that require winter dormancy should remain cold and dormant.

sections.heading: Watering
items: Dormant trees still need occasional moisture.
Check the soil periodically, particularly on trees that have been under cover for several weeks.
If the soil is becoming completely dry, water enough to bring it back to a slightly moist condition.
Don't keep dormant trees saturated. Good drainage is just as important in winter as it is during the growing season.

sections.heading: Planning for Spring
items: January is a great time to plan your spring repotting work.
Make a list of trees that need repotting and prioritize them based on species, age, health and root condition.
Make sure you have your soil components ready before spring arrives.
Order any bonsai pots, mesh, wire or other supplies you'll need.
Take the opportunity to review each tree and think about whether its current pot, soil and root system are still appropriate.

sections.heading: Winter Observation
items: Use the quiet period to study your trees rather than constantly working on them.
Look at branch structure and start thinking about your spring pruning and styling plans.
Check for damaged branches, rodents, pests or other winter problems when conditions allow.

focus: Protect, monitor and plan. There isn't much hands-on work to do, so use the downtime to keep your trees safely dormant and get organized for spring.

title: February Bonsai Checklist
intro: February marks the beginning of the transition toward spring. In some areas, repotting can begin this month, but timing should be based on the individual species, local temperatures and the tree's stage of dormancy.

sections.heading: Repotting Preparation
items: Start reviewing which trees will need repotting this spring.
Prioritize trees that are root-bound, have deteriorating soil, poor drainage or have simply outgrown their current containers.
Don't repot solely because the calendar says it's February. Wait until each species shows early spring activity, like swelling buds.
Deciduous trees are generally repotted as their buds begin to swell, before significant new growth emerges.
Most conifers follow soon after, once their buds swell and begin to move. Timing varies by species.

sections.heading: Bonsai Soil
items: Prepare your soil mixes ahead of time so everything is ready when repotting begins.
Use a mix appropriate to the species, container size and watering conditions rather than relying on one universal recipe.
Screen and grade your soil components before mixing.
Prepare enough soil for the trees you expect to repot, with some extra on hand for unexpected needs.
Store prepared soil somewhere dry and protected from freezing and excessive moisture.

sections.heading: Supplies
items: Check your supply of bonsai pots, drainage mesh, wire and tie-down materials.
Have pruning tools clean and ready to use.

sections.heading: Winter Protection
items: Continue protecting dormant trees from severe cold.
Keep monitoring moisture levels, particularly for trees kept under cover.
Check your shelters and containers after thaws and refreezes to make sure trees are still well protected.
Don't move trees into warm conditions prematurely. The goal is to protect them while allowing them to follow their natural seasonal cycle.

focus: Get ready for repotting rather than rushing into it. Prepare your soil, tools and containers now, then repot each tree when its species and local conditions indicate the timing is right.

title: March Bonsai Checklist
intro: March is when the bonsai collection begins transitioning from winter dormancy toward active growth. Depending on where you live, the timing can vary considerably from year to year, so bud development and weather conditions are more useful guides than the calendar.

sections.heading: Repotting
items: Start checking deciduous trees regularly for signs that the buds are beginning to swell.
For most deciduous species, repotting is best done when the tree is waking up but before the buds have opened and significant new growth begins.
Most conifers can be repotted as their buds swell and begin to move. Check the timing for each species.
Don't feel that you need to repot simply because it's March. A late winter or early spring can shift the timing by several weeks.
Avoid repotting during a period of severe or prolonged cold, particularly when the newly disturbed roots will be exposed to freezing conditions.
Keep records of every repot, including the date, soil mix, root work and container. Use them as a reference, but let the condition of the roots and the tree's vigour decide when it needs attention.
Younger, vigorous trees generally require repotting more frequently than older, established bonsai.

sections.heading: Root and Branch Pruning
items: Root pruning can be carried out as part of spring repotting when the tree is at the appropriate stage.
Preserve as much healthy fine-root structure as possible, particularly on recently collected or weaker trees.
Early spring can also be an excellent time for structural pruning while deciduous trees are still bare.
Avoid combining severe root reduction with heavy top pruning unless the tree is strong enough to tolerate both.

sections.heading: Wiring and Shaping
items: Bare deciduous trees are particularly easy to assess and wire because the branch structure is fully visible.
Early spring can be a good time for structural wiring and shaping on many species.
Check existing wire on trees that are beginning to grow and remove or adjust anything that is starting to bite into the bark.

sections.heading: Coming Out of Winter Protection
items: Don't remove winter protection just because March has arrived.
Many regions experience significant temperature swings during March, including sudden hard freezes after warm spells.
Gradually expose sheltered trees to outdoor conditions as the weather becomes more consistently suitable.
Pay particular attention to trees that have started swelling their buds. Newly activated buds are much more vulnerable to freezing than fully dormant trees.
Keep an eye on overnight temperatures and be prepared to provide additional protection when a hard freeze is forecast.

sections.heading: Fertilizing
items: Wait until a tree has clearly resumed active growth before beginning regular feeding.
Once growth starts, introduce fertilizer gradually rather than immediately applying heavy doses.
Newly repotted trees should be allowed time to recover before receiving strong fertilizer.

sections.heading: Pests and Disease
items: Begin inspecting trees carefully as they emerge from dormancy.
Check for overwintering scale, aphids, mites and other pests, as well as signs of fungal disease.
Early-season or dormant treatments can be useful for certain pests and diseases, but only use products that are appropriate for the species and follow the product label.
Choose a dry, relatively mild day for spraying and avoid applying treatments when freezing temperatures are imminent.

sections.heading: Collecting and Lifting
items: Early spring can be an excellent collection period for many deciduous species, provided the timing is right.
Aim to collect before significant bud break and leaf development.
Preserve as much fine, fibrous root as possible when lifting.
Some evergreens have a longer collection window, but the ideal timing varies by species.
Before collecting anything from the wild or public land, confirm that you have the necessary permission and that collection is legally permitted.

sections.heading: Seeds and Propagation
items: Deciduous seeds that have completed their required cold stratification can be sown.
Check the requirements of each species rather than assuming they all need the same stratification period.
If seeds have not yet been stratified, check the specific species requirements to determine whether there is still enough time to complete the process before spring sowing.

focus: Don't let the calendar dictate your timing. Watch the trees. When buds begin to swell and the weather starts to stabilize, begin the transition into spring work. Repot, prune and wire when the individual tree is ready, while continuing to protect the collection from unpredictable late-winter freezes.

title: April Bonsai Checklist
intro: April is when spring growth really begins to accelerate. Depending on where you live, the weather can still swing from winter-like conditions to warm spring days, so let the trees and the weather determine the pace of your work.

sections.heading: Repotting
items: Early April can still be a good repotting window for trees that haven't been done yet.
Use bud development and the tree's stage of growth as your guide rather than a fixed calendar date.
As deciduous trees begin opening their leaves, the ideal repotting window is generally closing.
Conifers are generally repotted on a similar schedule, as their buds swell and begin to move. Timing varies by species.
Avoid repotting trees that are already pushing substantial new growth unless there is a specific reason to do so.
After repotting, protect trees from unexpected cold snaps and strong winds while the roots recover.

sections.heading: Fertilizing
items: Trees that were not recently repotted can begin receiving regular fertilizer once active growth is underway.
Start with a relatively mild application and increase gradually as growth develops.
Newly repotted trees should not be fertilized immediately. Wait until they have recovered and are showing healthy new growth.
Avoid pushing recently repotted or stressed trees with heavy feeding.
Trees being grown for strong development may benefit from higher nitrogen early in the growing season, while more refined bonsai can be managed with a more balanced approach.
Hold off on feeding flowering trees until flowering has finished and the tree has had time to recover.

sections.heading: Monitoring Spring Growth
items: By April, most trees should be showing obvious signs of renewed activity, although the exact timing varies by species and year.
Watch for unusually early growth, since it is most at risk if a frost is forecast.
Protect newly emerging foliage when significant freezes are forecast.
Check junipers for signs of cedar-apple rust in damp spring weather, especially if apple or crabapple trees are nearby.
Increase watering gradually as temperatures rise and trees begin using more moisture.

sections.heading: Grooming and Development
items: Begin grooming trees that may be displayed later in the season.
Remove unwanted shoots, clean up dead growth and begin managing new growth as it develops.
Don't rush refinement work on trees that are still being developed. Strong spring growth can be valuable for building trunks and branches.
Take advantage of the clear structure of deciduous trees early in the season before the canopy becomes dense.

sections.heading: Seeds and Propagation
items: Continue sowing seeds once they have completed their required stratification.
April can be an excellent time to begin propagating many plants from cuttings.
Evergreen cuttings can often be taken from suitable previous-season growth.
When thinning or trimming suitable conifers and evergreens, save healthy cuttings rather than discarding useful material.
Use clean, healthy shoots with appropriate mature wood and prepare them promptly.

sections.heading: Air-Layering
items: Spring is a good time to begin air-layering suitable trees once they are actively growing.
Junipers, pines, Cryptomeria and other species can sometimes be air-layered successfully, but timing and technique vary by species.
Choose healthy branches with enough diameter and vigour to support the process.
Keep air layers consistently moist once established and monitor them throughout the growing season.

sections.heading: Shelter and Growing Area Cleanup
items: Give your greenhouse or winter shelter and the growing area a thorough spring cleanup before the season gets busy.
Remove old leaves, weeds and accumulated debris from benches and floors.
Clean and disinfect greenhouse surfaces, benches and tools where appropriate.
Pay particular attention to areas underneath benches where pests and fungal pathogens can overwinter.
If wooden benches or staging need treatment, use a product that is safe for an area where plants will be kept and allow adequate curing time before returning trees.

focus: Spring is underway, but don't assume every tree is on the same schedule. Finish repotting while individual trees are still at the right stage, begin feeding established trees as growth starts, take advantage of the propagation season, and stay alert for late frosts.

title: May Bonsai Checklist
intro: May is when growth takes off. Trees that looked quiet a few weeks ago are now pushing shoots, leaves and candles quickly, and each day brings something new to watch. Frost can still return in many regions, so keep protection handy until the danger has passed.

sections.heading: Watering and Sun
items: As growth speeds up, trees use much more water. Check the soil every day and water whenever it starts to dry.
Water thoroughly so it runs through the drainage holes, and avoid a light sprinkle that only wets the surface.
Watch trees under cover or in a greenhouse closely during warm spells, since they can dry out quickly.
Make sure any greenhouse vents and shade cloth work properly so sunny days don't overheat the space.

sections.heading: Late Frost Protection
items: New leaves are tender and can be damaged by a late frost, and the marks can stay on the leaves for the rest of the season.
Keep an eye on the forecast and be ready to move tender trees under cover on cold nights.
Trees with very early or soft growth, such as many maples, are the most vulnerable.
Bring tropical trees outdoors only once nights stay reliably warm.

sections.heading: Pinching and Shoot Care
items: Pinch back long, vigorous shoots on deciduous trees with your fingers as they extend, to keep the branch structure compact.
Pinch the candles on single-flush pines once they have stretched but before the needles open.
Pinch the soft growth tips on junipers as new shoots reach a few centimetres.
Let trees you are building up grow more freely, and save refinement for trees that are already developed.

sections.heading: Fertilizing
items: Keep feeding established trees. Start deciduous trees once their first leaves have firmed up.
Begin junipers as growth starts, and feed pines as their candles grow.
Hold off on strong fertilizer for trees that were repotted recently, until they show healthy new growth.

sections.heading: Seeds and Cuttings
items: Sowing is getting late in many regions, since seeds sown later in the season have less time to establish before winter.
Cuttings from many species can still be taken. Use clean, healthy shoots and keep them evenly moist.

sections.heading: Air-Layering
items: Air-layering deciduous trees can begin once they are in active growth and continue through summer.
Continue with evergreen layers already started, and keep every layer consistently moist.

sections.heading: Pests and Disease
items: Check new growth regularly for aphids, caterpillars and other early pests.
Check junipers for cedar-apple rust in damp weather, especially if apple or crabapple trees are nearby.

focus: Growth is fast and the weather is still unsettled. Water consistently, guard tender new leaves against a late frost, and pinch and feed as each tree's growth calls for it.

title: June Bonsai Checklist
intro: Summer starts now. In northern temperate climates, June brings the longest days of the year and the first real summer heat. Growth is at its peak.

sections.heading: Watering and Heat
items: Watering is the priority in June. Check your trees at least once a day and water whenever the surface of the soil begins to dry.
Evening is a good time to water. In hot, dry spells, water twice: once early in the morning before the sun hits the foliage, and again in the evening.
If it has rained hard during the day, check before watering, since the pots may already be well soaked.
Avoid watering in the heat of the midday sun.

sections.heading: Fertilizing
items: Growth is at its peak, so this is a good time to feed established trees regularly.
One simple rhythm is a slow-release organic granular feed at the start of the month, with a weak, high-potash liquid feed added once a week in between.
You can also use either one on its own: an organic granular feed replaced about monthly, or a diluted liquid feed every one to two weeks.
Don't feed weak, dry or freshly repotted trees.
Plan to stop nitrogen by mid-August so new growth hardens before winter.

sections.heading: Pinching and Pruning
items: Trees are pushing hard this month, so keep pinching new shoots to hold their shape.
On deciduous trees, let new shoots grow out to about five or six leaves, then cut back to about two to build fine, twiggy branching. Repeat through early summer.
Go lightly on crabapples and other flowering trees. They set next year's flower buds in summer, and heavy pinching removes them.
On single-flush pines, pinch or snap off about a third to a half of each strong candle before the needles open. Leave weak candles alone, and never remove the whole candle.

On two-flush pines, candle cutting usually comes in mid to late June, once the candles are fully stretched and the needles are just starting to separate. Cut strong candles back by about a third and medium ones by about half, and leave weak candles alone. Do this on strong, healthy trees only, and check the timing for your species.
On junipers, pinch new tips with your fingers to keep the foliage compact. Never strip a branch bare, since junipers rarely regrow from bare wood.

sections.heading: Pests and Disease
items: Aphids, both green and black, increase quickly now. Check the undersides of leaves regularly and treat at the first sign.
Keep checking junipers for cedar-apple rust in damp weather, especially if apple or crabapple trees are nearby.

sections.heading: Propagation
items: Keep doing air-layers on both evergreen and deciduous trees.

Early June is a good time for softwood cuttings. Chinese elm, zelkova and trident maple commonly root within a few weeks in good conditions. Japanese maples can be difficult to root from cuttings, so air layering is usually the more reliable choice.
Seedlings started in March should have two to three pairs of leaves by now and can be separated into their own pots.

sections.heading: Wiring
items: Wiring can be done any time of year, including June.
Be gentle to avoid damaging the soft new leaves on deciduous trees.

sections.heading: Leaf Pruning (Advanced, Optional)
items: From early June to mid-July, strong deciduous trees can be defoliated or partially leaf-pruned to encourage a second flush of smaller leaves. This is commonly done with maple, beech and sycamore.
This is for experienced growers and strong, healthy, well-fed trees only. Never do it on weak or freshly repotted trees.
On Japanese maple, remove leaves only partially.
Don't do it after mid-July, and skip it entirely where the growing season is short.

sections.heading: Tropical Trees
items: Move tropical trees outdoors once nights stay reliably warm. Start them in shade and move them to more sun over about a week, since direct sun straight after a winter indoors burns leaves.
Feed regularly while they are actively growing outdoors.
Summer is the time to prune hard and build structure on tropicals. They are also repotted in the warm months when growth is fastest, unlike hardy trees.
Try not to hard prune and repot the same tree in the same week.

focus: Growth is at its peak and summer heat has arrived. Water carefully, feed steadily, and shape new growth as it comes, while staying alert for pests.

title: July Bonsai Checklist
intro: July is usually the hottest stretch of the year. Most trees are growing well, and the main job is to keep them comfortable and steady through the heat.

sections.heading: Heat and Sun
items: Strong afternoon sun can scorch the leaves of delicate species such as maples and beeches. Give them morning sun and some shade in the hottest part of the day.
Shade cloth or a bench in the shadow of a larger plant can help where there is no natural shade.
Pots heat up in direct sun, which can stress the roots. Shade the containers, or set trees where the pots stay cooler.
Keep good air movement around trees so heat and humidity don't build up.

sections.heading: Watering
items: Check trees at least once a day and more often during heat waves. Small pots and shallow containers dry out the fastest.
Water thoroughly, and in hot weather water in the early morning and again in the evening if needed.
On very hot days, avoid wetting foliage in direct midday sun.

sections.heading: Fertilizing
items: Continue your regular feeding through July.
Skip feeding for weak, dry or freshly repotted trees, and plan to stop nitrogen by mid-August so growth hardens before winter.

sections.heading: Pinching and Shaping
items: Keep pinching new shoots on deciduous trees to maintain their shape and build finer branching, unless the tree is being grown out for thickness.
Pinch juniper tips as they regrow, and never strip a branch bare.
Check existing wire regularly. Fast summer growth can make wire bite into the bark, so remove or adjust it early.

sections.heading: Pests and Disease
items: Keep checking for aphids, mites, caterpillars and scale, especially under leaves. Treat early, before they spread.
Watch for fungal problems in warm, humid weather, and improve airflow where leaves stay damp.
Junipers near apple or crabapple trees can still get cedar-apple rust in damp weather.

sections.heading: Propagation
items: Softwood cuttings can still be taken in early summer. Once rooted, they are usually best left undisturbed until the following spring, since moving them late in the season gives them little time to establish before winter.

Check air layers for roots through the wrap. When they are well rooted, separate and pot them in a free-draining mix, and protect them from harsh sun and wind while they settle. Begin light feeding once they show new growth.

sections.heading: Advanced Work With a Closing Window
items: If you are doing leaf pruning (defoliation) on strong, healthy deciduous trees, or candle cutting on strong two-flush pines, the window closes around mid-July. Skip it for weak or recently repotted trees, and don't start it late in the month.

sections.heading: Looking Ahead
items: Late summer is a good time to think about autumn repotting for junipers and other suitable trees, and to order any soil or pots you'll need.

focus: Keep trees cool, watered and fed through the heat, keep shaping with light pinching, and finish any late summer leaf or candle work before the window closes.

title: August Bonsai Checklist
intro: August can bring some of the hottest and driest conditions of the growing season. The priority is keeping trees adequately hydrated while managing heat, strong sun and the rapid growth that can cause wire to bite into branches.

sections.heading: Watering and Heat
items: Check trees frequently during hot weather. Bonsai containers can dry out surprisingly quickly.
Water thoroughly when needed rather than relying on a fixed schedule.
During periods of extreme heat, trees in small pots or exposed locations may need attention more than once a day.
Water early in the day whenever possible, and check again later if conditions are exceptionally hot or windy.
Provide temporary shade for species that are prone to leaf scorch or heat stress.
Don't assume that rain has provided enough moisture. Heavy summer showers can wet the surface without thoroughly soaking the root ball.

sections.heading: Fertilizing
items: As summer progresses, gradually reduce the emphasis on high-nitrogen fertilizer, and plan to stop nitrogen by mid-August.
Trees that are still being developed may continue to need feeding, but excessive nitrogen late in the season can encourage soft, vigorous growth that has less time to mature before winter.
A balanced fertilizer or one with relatively less nitrogen can be useful as trees transition toward late-season growth.
Trees being grown for flowers and fruit may benefit from an appropriate phosphorus- and potassium-containing fertilizer, but avoid assuming that more is always better.
Adjust feeding according to the species, tree health and whether your goal is development, refinement, flowering or fruit production.

sections.heading: Wiring
items: Check every wired tree carefully.
August growth can cause branches and trunks to thicken quickly, particularly on vigorous trees.
Loosen or remove wire as soon as it begins to leave noticeable marks.
Don't assume that wire that was safely applied earlier in the season is still safe now.
Keep an eye on rapidly developing branches every few days during periods of strong growth.

sections.heading: Pests and Disease
items: Continue checking foliage, shoots and branches regularly for insects.
Treat pest problems when they appear rather than automatically spraying on a fixed schedule.
Pay particular attention to the undersides of leaves and tender new growth.
Use only treatments appropriate for the species and follow the product label.

sections.heading: Thinning and Needle Work
items: Early August is a good time to thin dense foliage pads on junipers, after summer pinching, so light and air reach the interior and the inner foliage doesn't die back.
In late August, once the new needles on two-flush pines have hardened, pull the oldest, browning needles, usually two or more years old, to let light and air into the inner buds.
Thin gradually, and don't strip weak branches all at once.

sections.heading: Tropical Trees
items: In colder regions, plan to bring tropical trees indoors in late August, before nights drop below about 12°C.
Move them gradually to a bright spot or under grow lights for about 12 to 14 hours a day, since sudden moves can cause leaf drop.
Check for spider mites and scale before bringing trees inside.

sections.heading: Air-Layering
items: Check air layers regularly for developing roots.
Once a layer has produced a strong, well-developed root system, it can eventually be separated and potted.
Don't rush the process. Give the new roots enough time to develop before removing the layer from the parent tree.
After separation, protect newly rooted layers from excessive heat, drying winds and direct sun while they establish.

sections.heading: Vacation Planning
items: Never underestimate how quickly a bonsai collection can dry out during a summer heat wave.
If you're going away, arrange for someone reliable to check and water the trees according to their actual needs.
Make sure the person understands that bonsai may require significantly more attention than ordinary garden plants.
Before leaving, group trees according to their watering requirements and provide shade where appropriate.
An automatic irrigation system can provide additional insurance, but it should be tested thoroughly before relying on it.

focus: Stay on top of watering, protect trees from excessive heat, monitor pests and wire closely, thin foliage and needles as the calendar calls for, and begin shifting from soft, nitrogen-driven growth toward mature late-season growth.
